summary: This informational document presents thoughts on how supporting HTTP Adaptive Streaming (HAS) affects Content Distribution Network Interconnection (CDNI). It gives the authors' analysis of the problem space and options for handling HAS in CDNI. It was used as input in the CDNI working group.

eli5.summary: Videos adjust quality to your connection, and many delivery networks must work together. This explores how they can cooperate.

questions: what is a manifest file in streaming
how does url signing work with adaptive streaming
subtitle: What happens to video chunks, manifests, logs and signed URLs when several CDNs must hand off HTTP adaptive streaming to each other.

tldr.problem: HTTP Adaptive Streaming splits video into many small chunks described by manifest files. Content Distribution Network Interconnection (CDNI) interfaces were being designed around single-file delivery, so chunk-heavy streaming raises questions for file management, request routing, logging, URL signing and purging.
tldr.mechanism: The authors set out the HAS aspects that matter to CDNI and, for six problem areas, list candidate options with their effect on the CDNI interfaces and their pros and cons, then recommend which to adopt now and which to defer.
tldr.outcome: They favour 'make it work' choices with little HAS-specific change to the CDNI interfaces, and defer fuller HAS awareness to a possible rechartering. The document is an independent submission, not a working group document.

facts.label: Log volume increase
facts.value: Two to three orders of magnitude

today: RFC 6983 is an Informational Independent Submission that has not been obsoleted or updated. It says it is not a working group document and that the RFC Editor makes no statement about its value for implementation or deployment. It relies on the problem statement in RFC 6707.

sections.title: Why HAS Matters for CDNI
sections.content:
RFC 6707 defines the problem space for Content Distribution Network Interconnection (CDNI), including delivery through interconnected CDNs of both HTTP progressive download and HTTP Adaptive Streaming (HAS). HAS is an umbrella term for HTTP-based streaming technologies in which a client switches between multiple bitrates depending on network conditions. Because it is built on HTTP, it is pull-based: the client actively requests content segments.

This document is the authors' analysis of the CDNI-HAS problem space and of options for dealing with it, and it ends with recommendations for the CDNI working group's initial charter, focused on 'making it work' rather than on nice-to-have optimizations that might delay deliverables. It states that it is not a working group document but was used as input to the working group's decision on HAS support.
sections.eli5: When a video is built from many small pieces fetched one at a time, sharing the job between two delivery companies gets trickier. This document asks what has to change.

sections.title: HAS Concepts That Affect CDNI
sections.content:
All HAS systems use chunking: splitting content into fixed-duration, independently decodable chunks, so a client can switch encodings at chunk boundaries. Chunks are stored either as segments, each a separate file with its own URL, or as fragments, all stored together in one file and addressed by a suffix such as a timestamp or byte range. Fragmentation is regarded as lower overhead, and segmentation as more flexible and easier to cache.

A client first fetches a manifest file (also called a Media Presentation Description) listing the chunks and where they are or how to address them. The RFC describes three ways to name chunk locations:

  • Relative URLs: the chunk is fetched relative to the manifest's location, so the same server delivers everything. This is easy to move between servers but offers no fallback and little flexibility.
  • Absolute URLs with redirection: the URL points at a request routing node that redirects the client. Maximum flexibility, but a redirect for every chunk loads the request routing system.
  • Absolute URLs without redirection: the URL points straight at a Surrogate. No per-chunk redirects, but the manifest must change whenever content moves.

Live content is harder than video on demand because manifests change with every chunk and are less cacheable. Stream splicing, such as ad insertion, means manifest rewriting must not disturb URLs or metadata that others rely on.
sections.eli5: The video is cut into small pieces and a menu tells the player where to find each one. The menu can say 'next door', 'ask the receptionist' or 'go straight to room 12'.

sections.title: Options for Files, Acquisition and Request Routing
sections.content:
For each problem area the RFC lists options with their effect on the CDNI interfaces. In file management, doing nothing forces the downstream CDN (dCDN) to store chunks as individual files, whereas allowing single-file storage of fragmented content needs full HAS awareness. A middle path adds an 'Access Correlation Hint' to the metadata. The authors recommend doing nothing for now (Option 1.1).

For content acquisition, per-chunk acquisition is flexible but creates transaction overhead. Single-file acquisition would need the dCDN to be HAS aware and significant metadata extensions. The authors recommend Option 2.1, which is sufficient to 'make HAS work'.

For request routing, Option 3.1 assumes no HAS awareness. Absolute URLs with redirection and some relative URLs work, but every chunk invokes the full inter-CDN request routing process. Option 3.2 lets the upstream CDN (uCDN) rewrite the manifest to point directly at the dCDN, with no change to the CDNI interfaces. Option 3.3 adds a second rewrite by the dCDN so it need not reveal its Surrogates. The authors recommend 3.1 with 3.2 as an optional uCDN-internal behaviour, and advise against 3.3.
sections.eli5: Should the second delivery company just treat each piece as a separate parcel, or learn how the pieces fit together? The authors say start simple, and let the first company rewrite the menu if it wants to save effort.

sections.title: Logging and Purging
sections.content:
HAS can multiply the number of log records by two to three orders of magnitude compared with regular HTTP delivery of a video, since logs are typically written per chunk rather than per content item. The RFC walks through each stage of the logging process that this affects. Its options are: do nothing (per-chunk logs), add a Content Collection ID and a Session-ID to help summarization, compress logs on the CDNI Logging interface, or require full HAS awareness with per-session logs.

The authors recommend per-chunk logging as a mandatory capability, the CCID and Session-ID mechanisms as an optional one, a generic way to customize reported log fields, and common compression such as gzip as optional. They defer per-session summarization to a possible rechartering.

For content purge, sending one purge request per file creates signaling overhead. A Purge-ID in the metadata can group files so a single request removes a whole content collection. The authors recommend Purge-IDs as an optional feature.
sections.eli5: Writing a diary line for every tiny piece makes a huge diary. The paper suggests giving all the pieces of one video a shared label so they can be summed up, and zipping the diary to make it smaller.

sections.title: URL Signing for Chunks
sections.content:
URL signing embeds authorization parameters and a message digest in a URL, so the delivering CDN can check that the request is legitimate. HAS complicates it: the expiry time in a signed manifest URL does not cover the many chunk URLs inside the manifest, which may be requested at widely varying times. How request routing rewrites the URL (DNS-based keeps it, HTTP-based changes it) and whether keys are symmetric or asymmetric also affect the trust model between the content service provider (CSP) and the CDNs.

The options are: sign only the top-level manifest (Option 5.1, which leaves chunks unprotected), flexible signing of the invariant URL portion by the CSP (5.2) or by the uCDN (5.3), an Authorization Group ID with an HTTP cookie (5.4), and two fully HAS-aware designs using a cookie (5.5) or CDN-signed manifests (5.6).

The authors consider doing nothing unsuitable. They recommend Option 5.4 where cookies are acceptable, because it needs no manifest manipulation, and otherwise Option 5.2 or 5.3. Options 5.5 and 5.6 are held back as future work because including HAS awareness would almost certainly delay the working group's milestones.
sections.eli5: A signed link is like a ticket. The trouble is that one ticket for the video's menu does not cover every little piece, so the paper compares ways to give each piece its own ticket or a wristband.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section is short. It states that the document does not discuss security issues related to HTTP or HAS delivery, because they are expected to be covered in the CDNI working group documents, including the CDNI framework. The security-relevant material in this document is the URL signing analysis in Section 3.5.
sections.eli5: This paper does not cover general safety for video delivery. Other documents are meant to do that.
